text: \textbf{R01 --- Review roadmap and central claim.} The strongest possible story is not simply ``Nash bargaining has desirable axioms.'' It is that a specific reference-surplus bargaining problem over general preference games can be solved reliably enough to improve a deployed LLM. The present evidence leaves two links unresolved: whether the practical training procedure realizes the proposed update, and whether adaptive game values help beyond fixed-reference Nash. Organize the paper around a falsifiable sequence: demonstrate residual within-objective preference misspecification; define the particular compromise being chosen; solve the finite game accurately; measure neural realization error; then evaluate independent trade-offs. Prioritize these links before expanding benchmark coverage. The comments below address substantive framing, correctness, and experimental design; intentionally unfinished tables and routine placeholders are not the focus.

\textbf{R02 --- Distinguish model misspecification from noisy labels.} The BT criticism in the next paragraph needs a probabilistic qualification. A BT model can assign nonzero probability to every observed binary outcome, including a sampled three-edge cycle; it cannot represent a population preference matrix whose strict majority relation cycles. Thus one contradictory annotation is not evidence that scalar reward modeling is misspecified. State the restriction at the level of $P_k$, not the requirement to satisfy every sampled label. Later compare a fitted BT model with held-out pair probabilities or repeated, order-balanced judgments. This distinction prevents a reviewer from dismissing the motivation as ordinary label noise, and makes clear what the game-based representation is intended to preserve.

\textbf{R03 --- The opening cycle currently changes the criterion between edges.} Relevance justifies $A\succ B$, completeness justifies $B\succ C$, and safety justifies $C\succ A$. This establishes conflict across attributes, but not necessarily a cycle within one of the separate objective oracles used by NBPO. Specify one fixed rubric under which all three comparisons occur, or explicitly separate attribute aggregation from residual within-rubric intransitivity. PROSPER already studies this distinction empirically \citep{zhang2026prosper}. For our data, audit complete triples under the actual training rubric and compare reproducible majority cycles with an appropriate BT/noise control. An illustrative example is useful, but the paper needs evidence that the representation problem remains after splitting feedback into the proposed objectives.

\textbf{R04 --- Equal bargaining power is a choice, not absence of priorities.} Prefer ``does not require user-specified scalarization weights'' or ``equal bargaining weight for the specified objectives'' to ``priority-free.'' Duplicating objective 1 changes its contribution from $\log s_1$ to $2\log s_1$, generally changing the policy; splitting one rubric into several correlated rubrics has a similar effect. Specify whether the bargaining parties represent objectives, judges, or stakeholder groups, and justify equal treatment at that level. A targeted sensitivity test should merge or duplicate an overlapping rubric and vary the disagreement policy. When varying the reference, distinguish its role as the fallback from its role as the opponent anchor. These are substantive design choices that affine invariance does not remove.

\textbf{R05 --- Attribute inherited ingredients and isolate the new technical increment.} INPO already eliminates an intractable normalizer through pairwise log-ratios \citep{zhang2025iterative}; PROSPER already combines KL-regularized adversarial comparisons, exponential reweighting, and regression-based policy fitting \citep{zhang2026prosper}. Therefore, presenting those ingredients individually as the main contribution invites an incremental-combination objection. Explain precisely what the nonlinear reference-surplus objective adds: the zero-surplus boundary and the coupled proximal subproblem that must be solved despite policy-dependent opponents. Identify which derivation addresses this additional difficulty and which computation implements it. The current exact theorem and conditional fixed-point argument do not by themselves establish that the stated practical alternation solves this subproblem; R11--R12, R14, and R16 explain the missing link.

\textbf{R06 --- Game-value improvement is not necessarily a direct win over the fallback.} Qualify this sentence and the corresponding introduction claim: the improvement is in $V_{k,\beta_k}$, not necessarily in $J_k(\pi,\piref)$. A concrete one-prompt example uses the cyclic margin matrix
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&.5&-.5\\-.5&0&.5\\.5&-.5&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
q=(.8,.1,.1),\quad p=(.25,.43,.32),\quad\beta=.25.
\]
Using $q$ as the reference gives $V(q)\simeq-.0517901$ and $V(p)\simeq-.0417293$, hence positive surplus $s(p)\simeq.0100608$, but $J(p,q)=-.0385$: the direct reference win rate is only $.4615$. This is a full-support, finite-temperature example under the same judge. Explain early why robustness-adjusted value is the intended notion of improvement, and evaluate direct wins separately. The limitation is more basic than the absence of per-prompt safety guarantees.

\textbf{R07 --- Provide a feasibility diagnostic and a defined failure outcome.} Joint strict improvement is a substantive assumption, particularly for conflicting objectives or an already strong reference. A constrained formulation makes the exact log problem well-defined when a feasible improvement exists; it does not discover one automatically or make an infeasible problem feasible. On each finite response pool, solve a phase-I problem $\max_{\pi,\tau}\tau$ subject to $s_k(\pi)\ge\tau$ for every $k$. Report its margin, then distinguish a genuinely nonpositive optimum from numerical or neural failure to realize a positive one. Include an intentionally conflicting panel with no strict common improvement and specify the returned status/policy. At the reference boundary, report rejection/stalling frequency. Floors and clipped inverse-surplus weights cannot create feasibility.

\textbf{R08 --- State exactly what the affine-invariance proposition covers.} The proposition correctly transforms completed utility functions and disagreement values together. It does not imply invariance to arbitrary judge calibration changes. At the primitive game level, if $\Delta'_k=c_k\Delta_k$, one must also set $\beta'_k=c_k\beta_k$ to preserve the opponent and obtain $V'_k=c_kV_k$. With temperature fixed, instead $V_{c\Delta,\beta}=cV_{\Delta,\beta/c}$, which changes the game. Also, scaling a centered preference margin beyond its probability range is a change of payoff units, not necessarily a realizable new probability oracle. Keep the algebraic guarantee, but explain this distinction before connecting it to judge-specific units or the rescaling experiment.

\textbf{R09 --- Keep three distributions distinct throughout the implementation.} The population proof optimizes over the full contextual simplex; a finite-pool solver optimizes categorical weights over sampled responses; the trained LLM defines a distribution over all possible responses. These are not interchangeable objects. Introduce separate notation for the exact inner solution, the finite-pool teacher, and the fitted neural policy. State which one generates each opponent and supplies each surplus in the dual update. This distinction is especially important with only four candidates and $R=1$: a highly accurate teacher solve can coexist with a poor neural projection. It should be possible to trace one outer update from sampled data to teacher weights to neural parameters without inferring undocumented computations.

\textbf{R10 --- Full-support identification does not follow from complete pairing within four candidates.} All six pairs among four sampled responses determine their relative probabilities, but do not control mass on unseen responses. For example, if only pair $(1,2)$ is observed with zero log-ratio-change target under a uniform three-response anchor, every policy $(a,a,1-2a)$ fits that pair while assigning different mass to response 3. State the support on which the regression-identification claim applies. Test candidate-pool expansion and fresh generations outside the training pool, and compare the exact teacher distribution with its neural realization. Separately qualify unbiasedness: the binary target has the displayed conditional mean under an exact opponent; the sampled, exponentially reweighted approximation in Appendix~\ref{app:labeling} requires its own error analysis (R34).

\textbf{R11 --- Critical: the displayed regression objective is not the objective used in the proof.} The square is outside the expectation, giving $(\E[\mathrm{residual}])^2$, whereas conditional-mean regression requires $\E[(\mathrm{residual})^2]$. These are mathematically different: large positive and negative residuals can cancel in the first expression; with symmetric ordered-pair sampling, that objective can even become uninformative. Move the square inside the expectation and verify the actual training loss, not only the typography. The appendix's argument that the regression minimizer recovers the desired pairwise target depends on minimizing squared error for individual examples. This is a substantive correctness issue because the policy-identification claim is otherwise unsupported.

\textbf{R12 --- Critical: fixed-point optimality does not establish convergence of the proposed alternation.} The appendix shows that an exact fixed point satisfies the inner optimality conditions, not that recomputing best responses reaches it. The iteration can actually be unstable. Use the RPS matrix $A$ in R06, with one objective, reference/outer anchor $q=(.34,.33,.33)$, $\beta=.25$, and $\eta\lambda=4$. The fixed-opponent map is
\[
T(p)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\log q+4A\operatorname{softmax}(\log q+Ap/\beta)\right).
\]
Its fixed point is approximately $(.33618258,.32907171,.33474571)$, but both tangent Jacobian eigenvalues are approximately $-1.33316$, implying local instability of undamped iteration. Full support holds, and this point improves value from about $-3.30\times10^{-5}$ at $q$ to $1.42\times10^{-5}$, so the joint-improvement assumption does not exclude the example. Replace ``produces a fixed point'' with the conditional statement proved. Supply a justified inner solver, an appropriate damping/contraction condition, or a different convergent scheme, and validate its residuals. Merely increasing $R$ is not a principled repair.

\textbf{R13 --- A bounded dual box can change the optimization problem.} The exact multiplier satisfies $\lambda_k^\star=1/s_k(\pi_{t+1})$. Therefore a legitimate positive surplus below $10^{-3}$ can require a multiplier above the implemented upper bound $10^3$; strict feasibility supplies no numerical lower bound on surplus. At a box boundary, projected stationarity need not imply the original condition $s_k-1/\lambda_k=0$. Report coordinatewise boundary-hit rates, unprojected KKT residuals, and sensitivity to the bounds. Explain whether the $5\times10^{-3}$ surplus floor changes the objective, only stabilizes estimation, or is used only in the rescaling diagnostic. Justify the box from a measured feasible margin where possible. Do not use clipped-solver convergence as a certificate for the original Nash proximal problem.

\textbf{R14 --- Reconcile Algorithm~\ref{alg:nbpo} with the reported computation.} The pseudocode calls \textsc{PolicyFit} at every dual iteration, but the configuration lists $40{,}000$--$300{,}000$ dual iterations and only 300 neural optimizer updates per stage. This suggests a finite-pool teacher solve followed by one neural fitting stage, rather than a fresh neural inner solve for every multiplier update. If that is the implementation, show it explicitly as a teacher solver plus a neural realization algorithm; if not, explain the actual update counts and costs. Recompute surplus, policy--opponent consistency, and KKT diagnostics after neural realization. A residual near $10^{-15}$ for the frozen teacher is not a certificate for the deployed LLM. Audit the implementation before deciding which algorithmic claim the paper can defend.

\textbf{R15 --- Test the acceptance safeguard near the boundary.} The existing disclaimer correctly avoids claiming a finite-sample guarantee, but positivity of noisy estimates is still the decisive practical acceptance criterion. With four comparators and small surpluses, an update can be falsely accepted or a genuinely feasible update repeatedly rejected. On known finite games, measure both error rates as functions of pool size, $L$, temperature, and true feasibility margin. Include all objectives jointly and report rejection frequency, especially at $t=0$. Keep the monitoring data separate from final evaluation; repeatedly using a held-out set to choose policies makes it validation data. A conservative simultaneous lower-confidence-bound check is worth testing, but do not apply a bounded-mean formula blindly to biased nonlinear game-value estimates.

\textbf{R16 --- Calibrate the theorem's contribution and computational meaning.} This is an exact Bregman proximal-point guarantee, not a convergence theorem for finite regression, one opponent refresh, a clipped dual, and empirical acceptance. State that distinction beside the headline claim. INPO already studies last-iterate convergence, and EGPO establishes linear convergence for a different regularized equilibrium problem \citep{zhang2025iterative,zhou2025egpo}; their rates are not comparable by exponent alone because targets and access assumptions differ. Here $T$ counts exact inner solves, not labels or neural steps, and all reported LLM configurations use $T=1$. Show finite-game convergence against total oracle/solver work, including an approximate-solve variant. A useful theoretical extension would relate an inner variational or primal--dual residual to outer error; preserving a last-iterate statement also needs a separate argument, for example control of approximate monotonicity.

\textbf{R17 --- Match information and computation, not only neural step counts.} The closest-method comparison needs separate accounting for unique semantic comparisons, order-swapped judge calls, generated response tokens, neural training compute, and hyperparameter trials. Equalizing 300 neural updates does not equalize the cost of candidate generation, opponent estimation, or repeated policy fitting. Report a fixed-label-budget comparison and a performance-versus-total-compute curve for NBPO, fixed-reference Nash, and the strongest preference-based competitors. For reward-model methods, use the same underlying preference information where feasible, charge reward fitting to their budget, and disclose extra pretrained supervision. If cached comparisons are reused across many numerical iterations, explain that reuse rather than counting every iteration as new evidence. These controls determine whether the optimizer is practically competitive.

\textbf{R18 --- Verify that the HT-MNPO baseline corresponds to the published method.} Heterogeneous MNPO trains an interacting population with players associated with different preference oracles \citep{wu2026mnpo}; independent single-objective runs are not automatically the same method. State the player count, oracle assignments, opponent mixture, joint update schedule, and how each reported checkpoint is obtained. Explain what ``single-objective HT-MNPO'' means in this implementation. Select the ``best corner'' using a prespecified validation criterion that does not access test results, and report whether any deployment-time mixture is allowed. The relevant distinction is one compromise policy versus a heterogeneous interacting population, not simply multi-objective versus single-objective learning. Consult the August 2026 revision, especially its heterogeneous extension.

\textbf{R19 --- Independent judges and diverse opponents answer different questions.} Judge independence is appropriate, but a fixed-reference win rate can miss precisely the exploitable weaknesses used to motivate adaptive opponents. Retain this deployment-oriented metric and add an independently judged cross-play matrix containing the reference, NBPO, fixed-reference Nash, and strong competing policies. Select adversarial comparators on a development pool and evaluate them on disjoint prompts/responses; include candidates outside the four-response training pool. Report a common regularized-game diagnostic under the same independently fixed evaluator as a complementary measure. Otherwise, the experiment can favor fixed-reference training by its metric while never testing whether adaptive training reduces vulnerability to other responses. Robustness and direct reference improvement should be reported as separate outcomes, as R06 demonstrates.

\textbf{R20 --- Explain the existing capability regression and benchmark score definitions.} Table~\ref{tab:general-benchmark-completion} reports a Llama IFEval decline from $.762$ to $.701$, or 6.1 percentage points, despite instruction following appearing in the training panel. This is a concrete transfer failure worth analyzing, not something that an average judged win rate resolves. Inspect failures by constraint type, answer length, and refusal behavior, and test a matched instruction-following/length control. Also distinguish official benchmark protocols from custom pairwise judging on benchmark prompts: converting MT-Bench or other benchmarks into reference-policy wins changes the metric and should be labeled explicitly. For small differences in judged scores, use paired prompt-level uncertainty and report evaluator disagreement rather than relying on three-decimal point estimates.

\textbf{R21 --- Evaluate the compromise rule relative to an attainable trade-off.} Average wins, worst-objective wins, and Nash welfare each express a different preference over outcomes; no single one proves that Nash is universally the best compromise. For the two-objective SafeRLHF panel, estimate an empirical trade-off curve using a reasonably tuned weight/constraint sweep and locate each method relative to that curve and the fallback. Use a common validation-only operating-point rule and disclose tuning effort. Combine this with objective-wise results so an aggregation advantage is distinguishable from simply training a stronger policy. The planned training-seed variation measures a different uncertainty source from finite evaluation prompts: report both, using paired prompt resampling and recomputing the worst-objective statistic within each replicate.

\textbf{R22 --- Make the adaptive-opponent falsification test central.} The present point estimates favor fixed-reference Nash in average reference wins ($.561$ versus $.556$); the appendix also reports higher minimum/average game surpluses ($.040/.061$ versus $.028/.056$). First confirm that these game surpluses use the same evaluator, temperature, and prompt set for both policies. The draft already acknowledges this negative result and proposes diagnostics; make those diagnostics the main mechanism experiment. Solve both targets accurately on identical finite matrices at the actual finite temperature, then measure the loss incurred by neural realization. Add a controlled transitive-to-cyclic family while maintaining joint feasibility, and evaluate diverse held-out comparators. The aim is to identify a regime where adaptivity helps, or establish why it does not, not to require NBPO to win every setting.

\textbf{R23 --- The current sign test is weaker than invariance of the implemented policy.} Specify whether the experiment rescales completed values or primitive payoffs; R08 gives the required temperature transformation for the latter. Exact dual weights transform as $\lambda'_k=\lambda_k/c_k$. Matching finite projected-gradient trajectories additionally requires transformed initial weights, coordinate bounds, floors, and coordinate step sizes $\gamma'_k=\gamma_k/c_k^2$. Compare full target magnitudes, opponent distributions, finite-pool policy KL, and neural outcomes, not only signs. Explain the identical utilitarian, Uniform-INPO, and MOPO rows: if they use a common frozen-score surrogate rather than each method's actual update, label that restriction. Do not infer algorithm-level scale sensitivity from an undocumented surrogate. Near-zero scores should be separated from substantive direction changes, and numerical covariance should not be described as robustness to arbitrary judge miscalibration.

\textbf{R24 --- Separate the aggregation rule from the order of aggregation over prompts.} PROSPER's adversarial objective weights are prompt-dependent, whereas NBPO's inverse-surplus weights operate on objective values averaged over prompts \citep{zhang2026prosper}. Thus the comparison changes both the compromise criterion and the ability to compensate for poor performance on one prompt with improvement on another. Write the two objectives side by side and include a two-prompt example showing the distinction. Retain a faithful prompt-wise PROSPER baseline and the matched global-maxmin control over NBPO's game values. Without this separation, an empirical difference cannot be attributed specifically to Nash bargaining. Make clear that the individual-rationality guarantee is about population-average objective game values, not every prompt or every stakeholder.

\textbf{R25 --- Correct the substantive classification of MOPO and discuss RACO.} The preceding paragraph incorrectly includes MOPO among methods requiring scalar objective rewards or transitive preference models. MOPO explicitly uses pairwise preferences without a point-wise reward assumption; its June 2026 revision also refreshes a lagged reference and constraint schedule \citep{agnihotri2026mopo}. Distinguish its primary-objective/constraint selection and reference-based comparisons from NBPO's symmetric surplus bargaining and policy-dependent adversarial opponent. Also position RACO, a recent reward-free method for conflicting objectives using preference-loss updates \citep{chen2026raco}; reward-free training alone is not new. A matched RACO comparison is useful, but distinguish its DPO-style representation from unrestricted cyclic preference modeling. This correction is necessary for a credible novelty argument, not merely broader citation coverage.

\textbf{R26 --- Compare against the current Nash-welfare literature at the level of the optimized object.} The \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.05006v2}{September 7, 2026 revision of Zhong et al.}, now titled \emph{Provable Pluralistic Alignment: Multi-Party RLHF under Offline Human Feedback}, includes disagreement-adjusted bargaining and separately treats general preferences through a von Neumann formulation. Update the bibliography/positioning rather than relying on the older title. Explain that its welfare analysis concerns learned party rewards, Nash-MTL bargains over immediate gradient improvements, and NBPO bargains over robust policy-value surpluses. Nash welfare, inverse-improvement weighting, and reference subtraction are therefore not individually sufficient novelty. Besides fixed-reference Nash, fit scalar rewards to the same comparisons and apply Nash aggregation as a controlled baseline; this isolates the incremental value of the game representation without confounding it with the welfare choice.

\textbf{R27 --- Compare with a strong bargaining alternative, not only unnormalized maxmin.} Table~\ref{tab:rule-guarantees} characterizes the particular rules as defined; it does not establish that Nash is the only reasonable scale-invariant compromise. The Pareto counterexample for maxmin exploits a dominated member of an optimum set, so a Pareto-refining tie-break can remove that failure. Consider a normalized relative-improvement maxmin or Kalai--Smorodinsky control, using each objective's attainable improvement above the fallback; \citet{han2026fair} is a directly relevant 2026 treatment, and \citet{kalai1975} supplies the classical alternative. Explain the additional ideal-point estimation cost and use validation data fairly. Comparing Nash with this stronger alternative would test the substantive bargaining choice; demonstrating that unnormalized maxmin depends on units mainly confirms a known algebraic property.

\textbf{R28 --- Diagnose the failure cases already present in the objective-wise table.} In Table~\ref{tab:objectivewise-appendix}, TL;DR conciseness has NBPO surplus $-.001$. On SafeRLHF, NBPO's vector $(.118,.101)$ is strictly dominated in both reported coordinates by PROSPER $(.151,.116)$, utilitarian aggregation $(.157,.138)$, and both maxmin controls. These estimates do not refute the exact population theorem: finite proximal regularization, estimation, and neural error can all prevent its limiting outcome properties from appearing. They do prevent interpreting this trained policy as empirically individually rational or Pareto efficient on these diagnostics. Verify the comparisons under identical prompts, evaluator, comparators, and temperature with paired uncertainty. Then localize the gap to finite-pool optimization or neural realization, and discuss the verified failure cases in the main results rather than only the appendix.

\textbf{R29 --- Complete the planned split change before using validation as evidence of generalization.} The table explicitly distinguishes the current pair-level split from a planned prompt-level split. The reason is substantive: six unordered pairs can share the same four responses, so random pair splitting allows training and validation to contain overlapping prompts and candidates. Group by source prompt before generating or allocating pairs, keep swapped orders together, and remove cross-split duplicates. Explain which existing numbers use the old split and which use the corrected protocol; do not combine them as one held-out evaluation. The 657-prompt main panel and 698-prompt diagnostic panel also need explicit identities/overlap so apparent metric differences can be separated from changes in evaluation population.

\textbf{R30 --- Separate changing the training temperature from changing the evaluation ruler.} The temperature study is only interpretable if every trained policy is also evaluated at a common fixed diagnostic temperature and under common independent metrics. Evaluating each policy with its own $V_{k,\beta_k}$ changes both the optimizer and the quantity being compared. Show a small train-temperature by evaluation-temperature comparison, while retaining one prespecified common evaluation column for the main conclusion. Opponent entropy is useful but does not diagnose correctness: with only four candidates, concentration may reflect noisy margin estimates rather than meaningful adversarial pressure. Pair the temperature sweep with comparator-pool/$L$ scaling and exact-versus-estimated opponent error on a finite game, instead of reading lower entropy as evidence that robustness improved.

\textbf{R31 --- Critical diagnostic: the reported regression fit may not beat predicting zero.} The existing target RMS of $8.56$ implies zero-output MSE $8.56^2=73.2736$, slightly below the reported fitted MSE $73.9$, if both use identical examples, targets, and weighting. This would mean the learned log-ratio change is no better in this metric than making no update. First reconcile the measurement conventions and report initial/final loss against the same zero baseline. Then separate error against the conditional-mean target from irreducible binary-label variance using the frozen preference matrices, and run an oracle-target regression control. Vary target magnitude, neural optimization budget, and pair coverage. A very accurate frozen dual cannot compensate for failure to realize its target in the language model; resolve this before interpreting the main optimizer claim.

\textbf{R32 --- Make the planned cycle-conditioned analysis distinguish misspecification from estimation noise.} Define the cyclicity statistic and subset threshold before examining which method wins. Report strict majority cycles separately from ties, presentation-order disagreement, and unstable edges. Repeat a subset of judgments under a specified randomness source: rerunning an identical deterministic judge prompt does not create independent evidence. Fit a BT projection to the same comparison matrices and compare original-matrix versus projected-matrix bargaining under matched budgets. Combine this with a synthetic sweep of cycle strength/frequency at finite $\beta$ and full-support references, while preserving joint feasibility. These controls test whether nontransitivity itself explains adaptive-opponent performance; merely stratifying noisy four-response matrices can instead select difficult prompts or judgment variance.

\textbf{R33 --- Make label provenance and rubric identity auditable for every reported run.} The note distinguishing Beaver-head precursor runs from prompted comparisons is important. Scalar-head-induced rankings are transitive by construction and therefore cannot substantiate the paper's claim about preserving within-objective cycles. Attach an unambiguous label-source identifier to each checkpoint/result and ensure that the main adaptive versus fixed-reference comparison differs only in the intended component. Also provide the actual per-panel rubric mapping: the prose lists correctness/coherence, whereas some tables use honesty, truthfulness, and instruction following. This is not just terminology because changing or splitting an objective changes both the preference matrices and the bargaining outcome. Measure rubric agreement and show independent evaluator results separately before pooling them.

\textbf{R34 --- Quantify the approximation introduced before binary regression even starts.} An unbiased estimate of $m$ does not give an unbiased opponent after exponentiation and normalization, nor an unbiased log-sum-exp game-value estimate. The practical target therefore refers to a random finite-pool opponent, not automatically to the population $Q_k^\pi$ in the proof. With $L=4$ and four reference candidates, this discrepancy may be important, especially at small $\beta$ and near zero surplus. On a finite game with known preference probabilities, vary $L$, comparator count, and temperature; measure opponent-distribution error, target bias/variance, surplus bias, and final policy error against exact quantities. State whether labels used to select/reweight opponents are reused in the target; use fresh labels or cross-fitting to diagnose selection effects. Separate this estimation error from neural regression error and numerical dual accuracy.
